companyDossiers.name: Neuralink
companyDossiers.summary: A laboratory insertion method became a company-built implant, robot, microfabrication process and wireless system. Later decoding licenses form a separate university connection.

stages.title: Research roots
stages.text: Philip Sabes brought neural-systems research and a UCSF–Berkeley flexible-probe insertion collaboration. The 2019 sewing-machine preprint documents its animal-stage mechanism.

stages.title: Translation
stages.text: Sabes joined Neuralink full time in 2017; the lab explicitly says the company refined its approach. Rapoport was also a co-founder. Stanford later licensed speech-decoding IP to Neuralink.

stages.title: Interface built
stages.text: The 2019 research platform paired independently inserted flexible threads with custom amplifiers, digitization and USB readout. The 2024 N1 design integrates a wireless implant and surgical robot.

timeline.title: Academic-to-company transition
timeline.text: Sabes left his UCSF role for full-time Neuralink work.

timeline.title: Academic insertion precursor published
timeline.text: The sewing-machine preprint describes flexible probes placed with a separate stiff insertion needle in rats.

timeline.title: Integrated research platform
timeline.text: Neuralink published its 3,072-channel maximum research configuration, with 96 threads carrying 32 electrodes each.

timeline.title: Human N1 engineering update
timeline.text: The company describes a 1,024-electrode implant on 64 threads, wireless readout and R1 placement.

timeline.title: Stanford speech-decoding license disclosed
timeline.text: A published paper lists Neuralink among Stanford’s licensees.

changes.title: Insertion becomes a manufacturing-and-surgery system
changes.text: Flexible electrodes require placement tooling, vision, packaging and quality control; electrode count alone omits these company engineering changes.

changes.title: Research maximum is not a human product progression
changes.text: The 2019 3,072-channel rodent/USB system and 2024 1,024-electrode human N1 are different configurations; the lower N1 count is not evidence of a failed doubling law.

gaps: No academic hardware license agreement was established for the sewing-machine link.
A Stanford decoding license does not establish that a specific published decoder runs in the N1.
This is a selected technical founder history, not a complete founder roster.

companyDossiers.name: Precision Neuroscience
companyDossiers.summary: Precision combines founder experience in implanted BCIs with surface-array engineering, its own foundry and a national-laboratory longevity collaboration.

stages.title: Research roots
stages.text: Rapoport’s MIT engineering/medical training and earlier Neuralink co-founding are documented personnel links. The array design paper separately shows a 529-site research design used to choose dimensions for the nominal 1,024-channel version.

stages.title: Translation
stages.text: Precision was founded in 2021. It acquired a MEMS foundry through Precision BioMEMS in 2023, entered a three-year LLNL longevity CRADA in 2024, and hired Tolosa in 2025.

stages.title: Interface built
stages.text: Flexible arrays record across the cortical surface. Density and modular area coverage are separate scaling mechanisms. The paper’s micro-slit delivery evidence is animal/cadaver work; human results are intraoperative.

timeline.title: Company founded
timeline.text: LLNL’s collaboration announcement dates Precision’s start to 2021.

timeline.title: Manufacturing acquired
timeline.text: A Texas foundry becomes an internal fabrication capability through Precision BioMEMS.

timeline.title: Longevity collaboration
timeline.text: LLNL and Precision announce a three-year CRADA.

timeline.title: Four-array intraoperative recording
timeline.text: Company reports 4,096 electrodes across four arrays; announcement followed on May 28.

timeline.title: Temporary-array clearance
timeline.text: Layer 7-T clearance covers use for less than 30 days.

timeline.title: Design and implantation paper
timeline.text: Published work details array geometry, modularity, preclinical insertion and a five-patient intraoperative pilot.

changes.title: Own the fabrication process
changes.text: The acquired foundry adds control of MEMS production and iteration; this is a concrete organizational change rather than a larger electrode count.

changes.title: Choose density with physiology and manufacturing
changes.text: The development arrays varied electrode sizes; the design was selected using impedance, manufacturing reliability and signal correlations.

changes.title: Engineer longer life
changes.text: The LLNL program addresses thin-film longevity; manufacturing transfer of resulting methods was announced as intended.

gaps: Shared founders or hires do not prove that Neuralink technology was transferred to Precision.
Temporary Layer 7-T clearance is not authorization of a fully implanted chronic wireless BCI.
The nominal 1,024 design includes reference and stimulation-optimized sites; it is not 1,024 independently isolated neurons.

companyDossiers.name: Paradromics
companyDossiers.summary: Paradromics’ origin story connects a collaborative microwire/CMOS platform to company packaging and later licensed speech-BCI IP; these are different kinds of relationship.

stages.title: Research roots
stages.text: Angle founded the company in 2015. A 2020 collaboration involving Paradromics and Melosh’s Stanford group separated flexible microwire bundles from dense silicon readout chips.

stages.title: Translation
stages.text: The collaboration is documented by a paper and university account. Separately, a 2025 disclosure identifies UC-owned speech-BCI IP licensed by Paradromics. Neither fact establishes a Stanford hardware spinout.

stages.title: Interface built
stages.text: Connexus packages 421 microelectrodes in a brain module connected to a chest transceiver. The company describes inductive power and optical communication across the skin.

timeline.title: Company founded
timeline.text: Official company profile dates the start of Angle’s company.

timeline.title: Microwire–CMOS platform published
timeline.text: A multi-institution paper demonstrates the architecture in preclinical recording.

timeline.title: Temporary human recording milestone
timeline.text: The company’s history and 2026 announcement distinguish earlier temporary recording from its later chronic implant.

timeline.title: Speech-BCI license disclosed
timeline.text: UC Regents patent applications include IP licensed by Paradromics.

timeline.title: Connect-One study authorized
timeline.text: Company announces FDA authorization for its investigational clinical study.

timeline.title: Chronic implant announced
timeline.text: Company reports the first chronic Connect-One implantation at the University of Michigan.

changes.title: Separate sensing from readout geometry
changes.text: The precursor’s wire-bundle/CMOS connection lets tissue-facing mechanics and silicon electronics be designed separately.

changes.title: Turn a recording architecture into an implant system
changes.text: Connexus adds implanted packaging, lead routing, chest transceiver and wireless power/data; these carry different constraints from benchtop channel capacity.

gaps: Angle’s exact doctoral/postdoctoral mentorship was not established by the inspected primary sources; no mentor edge is asserted.
Co-authorship and joint development do not establish an exclusive Stanford hardware license.
The speech-IP disclosure leaves agreement terms and Connexus implementation unspecified.
Do not equate the 2025 temporary human experiment with the 2026 chronic trial implant.

companyDossiers.name: Blackrock Neurotech
companyDossiers.summary: Blackrock inherits a long university and supplier lineage, then adds manufacturing, acquisition hardware and translational systems. Its corporate history is separate from BrainGate’s academic clinical program.

stages.title: Research roots
stages.text: Normann’s Utah Array preceded the company. Solzbacher’s Utah work addressed reliability and manufacturability. The earlier Bionic Technologies supplier business was acquired by Cyberkinetics in 2002.

stages.title: Translation
stages.text: Solzbacher and Gerhardt founded Blackrock around 2007–2008. Its history links the company to Cyberkinetics’ research business; SEC records specify the transferred assets and research license. Utah technology was also licensed.

stages.title: Interface built
stages.text: Blackrock supplies arrays and acquisition systems used by academic teams. Wireless home-use research commercialized a Brown transmitter; a later Stanford speech-IP license represents a decoder connection.

timeline.title: Utah Array development
timeline.text: Normann’s silicon-array work predates Blackrock.

timeline.title: Bionic business acquired
timeline.text: Cyberkinetics gained research-device staff, manufacturing and IP.

timeline.title: Blackrock formed
timeline.text: Utah’s interview says 2007; the company dates founding to 2008.

timeline.title: Research-business assets transferred
timeline.text: Contemporaneous filings record the transaction, while distinguishing retained clinical IP.

timeline.title: Wireless home-use study reported
timeline.text: Brown describes a commercialized transmitter used with existing percutaneous array connectors.

timeline.title: Speech-decoding license disclosed
timeline.text: Stanford’s license to Blackrock appears in a published paper’s disclosures.

changes.title: Reliability and production are part of scaling
changes.text: Solzbacher’s account stresses manufacturability, stable materials and complete acquisition systems, rather than simply adding silicon needles.

changes.title: Electrode arrays and readout are separate products
changes.text: NeuroPort acquisition capacity can exceed the wired contacts in a single implant. A study’s implanted sites, acquired channels and selected decoder inputs need separate labels.

changes.title: Wireless has more than one meaning
changes.text: The Brown transmitter used in this research attaches outside the skin to a connector; that is not equivalent to a fully implanted package.

gaps: Do not label the 2008 transaction as purchase of all Cyberkinetics or all BrainGate clinical IP.
BrainGate2 is an academic research program, not another name for Blackrock.
A research hardware supplier’s device count is not a complete commercial BCI performance measure.

companyDossiers.name: Synchron
companyDossiers.summary: Synchron grew from Melbourne’s multidisciplinary endovascular research into a company-built digital-control system; its principal scaling choice is the access route, not a large electrode count.

stages.title: Research roots
stages.text: Oxley explored the idea during doctoral work in 2011. He and Opie formed the Vascular Bionics Laboratory; Opie brought experience from a bionic-eye project.

stages.title: Translation
stages.text: Synchron was founded in 2012 as a commercial vehicle. University, Royal Melbourne Hospital, Florey and company contributors co-developed Stentrode.

stages.title: Interface built
stages.text: Electrodes on a stent acquire cortical signals from a blood vessel. The human system routes signals to an implanted chest unit and an external receiver; early digital control combined neural clicking with eye tracking.

timeline.title: Doctoral idea explored
timeline.text: Oxley begins investigating the endovascular route as a Melbourne PhD student.

timeline.title: Company formed
timeline.text: The university commercialization case dates Synchron’s founding to 2012.

timeline.title: Preclinical stent-electrode paper
timeline.text: Sheep experiments establish the early endovascular recording platform.

timeline.title: First human implant in early cohort
timeline.text: Melbourne’s subsequent report dates one of the first two implants to August 2019.

timeline.title: First-two-user report
timeline.text: Participants used a 16-sensor system for home digital control with eye tracking.

timeline.title: SWITCH safety follow-up
timeline.text: A four-participant study reports 12-month follow-up of the fully implanted endovascular system.

changes.title: Make vascular delivery the access strategy
changes.text: The stent scaffold carries electrodes through a catheter-accessible route near motor cortex. It changes where signals are sampled and the surgical workflow.

changes.title: Translate a signal into a useful click
changes.text: The early interface used a small command set with eye-tracking software; this separates practical access from free-form speech or continuous multidimensional motor decoding.

changes.title: Move from animal recording to implanted daily-use components
changes.text: The human system adds subcutaneous lead routing, chest electronics and external receiving/control equipment.

gaps: No exclusive university-to-company license contract was located in these sources; co-development is the supported label.
The bionic-eye link is Opie’s experience, not evidence of retinal-patent transfer.
A 16-contact endovascular array does not measure the same signals or coverage as 16 penetrating intracortical contacts.
The four-person SWITCH result is a small clinical study, not proof of indefinite vascular or device durability.

sources.limit: Company progress report; numbers concern the human N1 design, not the 2019 research system.

sources.title: Inside the operating room: Doctors test a revolutionary brain-computer implant
sources.evidence: MIT reports Rapoport’s EECS PhD in 2011 and MD in 2013, and identifies him as co-founder of Neuralink and Precision.
sources.limit: Alumnus biography; does not establish transfer of MIT or Neuralink IP to Precision.

sources.title: Precision Neuroscience — Our vision
sources.evidence: Leadership biographies identify Benjamin Rapoport and Michael Mager as co-founders and describe technical leaders’ prior roles.

sources.title: LLNL and Precision Neuroscience collaboration aims to develop next-generation neural implants
sources.evidence: A three-year CRADA targets thin-film implant longevity; Precision intends to transfer resulting methods to Precision BioMEMS. The article dates Precision’s founding to 2021.
sources.limit: Manufacturing transfer is an intention, not evidence it has been completed.

sources.title: Precision Neuroscience Expands Leadership Team with Key Hires from Meta and FDA
sources.evidence: Tolosa joins as SVP of R&D after LLNL polymer-array work, Neuralink co-founding and leadership of neural-interface fabrication, and Meta wearable work.
sources.limit: Historical employment is not an IP transfer.

sources.title: Precision Neuroscience Acquires U.S. Manufacturing Facility and Receives FDA Breakthrough Device Designation
sources.evidence: Precision acquired a Texas MEMS foundry through wholly owned Precision BioMEMS and retained the manufacturing team.

sources.title: Minimally invasive implantation of scalable high-density cortical microelectrode arrays for multimodal neural decoding and stimulation
sources.evidence: The paper documents 529-site development arrays and a nominal 1,024-channel design, modular cortical coverage, animal/cadaver micro-slit insertion, and a five-patient intraoperative pilot.
sources.limit: Human chronic reversibility was not demonstrated. Nominal 1,024 comprises 977 recording-sized, 42 stimulation-optimized and five reference electrodes.

sources.title: FDA K242618 — Layer 7-T cortical interface
sources.evidence: Clearance covers the Layer 7-T electrode array for temporary use lasting less than 30 days.
sources.limit: Not market authorization for a complete chronic wireless BCI.

sources.title: Precision Neuroscience Announces World Record for Number of Electrodes Placed On Human Brain
sources.evidence: Four 1,024-electrode arrays were used for intraoperative recording in April 2024.
sources.limit: Company-reported acute placement/recording; not 4,096 chronic single-neuron channels.

sources.title: Paradromics — Company
sources.evidence: Names Matt Angle as founder and CEO; company history includes Austin expansion, preclinical Connexus work, and human milestones.
sources.limit: The current company page does not specify Angle’s doctoral or postdoctoral mentors.

sources.title: Paradromics Inc. — official company profile
sources.evidence: The official company profile dates founding to 2015 and identifies founder Matt Angle.

sources.title: Bringing silicon computing power to the brain
sources.evidence: Stanford reports microwire bundles contacting CMOS chips and identifies Stanford, Paradromics, the Francis Crick Institute, UCL and ETH collaborators.
sources.limit: A collaborative preclinical platform; not proof of a hardware license or identical Connexus implementation.

sources.title: Massively parallel microwire arrays integrated with CMOS chips for neural recording
sources.evidence: Obaid and colleagues separate the microwire bundle from CMOS readout; Angle and Melosh are co-authors.
sources.limit: Co-authorship supports collaboration, not a mentor relationship.

sources.title: An instantaneous voice-synthesis neuroprosthesis — author manuscript
sources.evidence: Competing interests identify Stanford speech-decoding patent 12008987 as licensed to Blackrock and Neuralink, and UC Regents speech-BCI applications 63/461,507 and 63/450,317 as including IP licensed by Paradromics.
sources.limit: Exact license dates, exclusivity, contract terms and incorporation into shipping company products are not disclosed. Source is a published paper disclosure, not the agreements.

sources.title: Paradromics — Connexus
sources.evidence: Describes the 421-microelectrode brain module, implanted lead and chest transceiver, inductive power and optical data transmission.
sources.limit: A design description; intended long service life is not observed decade-long human durability.

sources.title: Paradromics Receives FDA Approval for the Connect-One Clinical Study with the Connexus Brain-Computer Interface
sources.evidence: Announces authorization of the investigational Connect-One study.
sources.limit: Study authorization is not commercial marketing approval.

sources.title: Paradromics Completes First Human Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) Implantation
sources.evidence: Reports the first chronic Connect-One implantation at the University of Michigan; distinguishes the temporary 2025 recording milestone.
sources.limit: Announcement date; exact procedure date is not supplied here.

sources.title: Brain Trust: A Q&A with Florian Solzbacher
sources.evidence: Describes Normann’s Utah Array, Solzbacher joining Utah in 2004 and engineering improvements; dates company formation to 2007 and subsequent Utah licensing.
sources.limit: Formation year conflicts with Blackrock’s own 2008 account; retain the discrepancy.

sources.title: Blackrock Neurotech — Our story
sources.evidence: Names Solzbacher and Gerhardt as founders in 2008 and describes acquisition from Cyberkinetics.
sources.limit: The company summary says “acquires Cyberkinetics”; contemporaneous SEC documents specify a research-business asset transaction and retained clinical IP.

sources.title: Cyberkinetics — Form 8-K, research-business disposition
sources.evidence: Reports the May 15, 2008 disposition of research-business assets to I2S Micro Implantable Systems Inc.

sources.title: Cyberkinetics — Form 10-Q, asset-purchase agreement terms
sources.evidence: Describes research inventory, fixed assets, engineering subcontracts and a research-products license; Cyberkinetics retained clinical neural-interface IP and approvals, including BrainGate and NeuroPort.
sources.limit: This filing describes transaction terms; read with the later closing report.

sources.title: Cyberkinetics — Form 8-K, acquired Bionic Technologies business
sources.evidence: Describes its 2002 Bionic Technologies acquisition, bringing engineering staff, manufacturing facilities and IP; continuing BIONIC recording-array and acquisition products.
sources.limit: The same filing uses both “late 2002” and “August 2002”; retain year precision.

sources.title: Blackrock — NeuroPort data acquisition
sources.evidence: Describes configurable neural-signal acquisition, real-time closed-loop use and up to 512 recording channels.
sources.limit: Acquisition capacity is not the number of contacts in every implanted Utah array.

sources.title: Researchers demonstrate first human use of high-bandwidth wireless brain-computer interface
sources.evidence: Brown reports wireless home-use research using the Brown Wireless Device, commercialized by Blackrock.
sources.limit: Wireless transmitter mounts on percutaneous connectors; not a fully implanted N1-like package.

sources.title: Giving people with severe paralysis the power to communicate using their thoughts
sources.evidence: University commercialization case identifies Synchron, founded in 2012, as the commercial vehicle for Stentrode development with Melbourne partners.

sources.title: Moving with the power of thought
sources.evidence: Reports recruitment of Nicholas Opie from the bionic-eye project and engineering of electrodes onto a collapsible nitinol stent.
sources.limit: Bionic-eye work is a personnel-expertise link, not evidence of transferred retinal-device IP.

sources.title: Translating thought into action
sources.evidence: Oxley explored the idea as a Melbourne PhD student in 2011; he and Opie formed the Vascular Bionics Laboratory. The article describes 16 sensors and first two human users with eye-tracking-assisted digital control.
sources.limit: Do not repeat the article’s speculative permanent lifetime claim or treat its 2025 approval forecast as achieved.

sources.title: Minimally invasive endovascular stent-electrode array for high-fidelity, chronic recordings of cortical neural activity
sources.evidence: Oxley and colleagues report endovascular cortical recording in a preclinical sheep model.
sources.limit: This is preclinical evidence; publication precedes human use.

sources.title: Assessment of safety of a fully implanted endovascular brain-computer interface for severe paralysis in four patients: SWITCH study
sources.evidence: Four implanted participants were followed for 12 months in the SWITCH safety study.
sources.limit: Small single-arm study, including the early participants; not a market authorization or an independent large replication.
